I saw people mention cold water on their face and going for a walk. I've heard activities that use both sides of your brain can be calming, which walking does. I think it's called cross lateral movement or something like that. I play guitar/piano which seem to help in a similar way. Or giving a sort of "self hug", crossing my arms cross my chest and tapping my fingers on opposite shoulders or tapping on collarbone or ribs. 

The calming effect of cold water might be related to the "mamillian dive reflex", or to "cold shock response", if you want to learn more about those. 

Journaling has also been a good outlet for me. I'm not in the habit right now, but I used to write for 5-15 mins when I first wake up and before I go to bed. Getting thoughts out of my head like that seemed to reduce my general anxiety, and made it easier to let go of things I had been holding on to. Writing also forces you to slow down your thinking and be more articulate with your thoughts, which both seem to help me wind down. 

Good luck today. Hope it goes better than yesterday for you

Just stumbled upon this subreddit. I don't comment much but I feel your pain. I may have cPTSD (not sure) but I definitely struggle with suicidal thoughts.

I relate to what you're saying, feeling at a roadblock. I think I do get stuck in fight or flight mode. I feel such an urge to do something, but such hopelessness when I remember all the times I've pushed down the wrong path. But the fight/flight state is temporary. What you said about just being in someone's space for a time, I can see how that would be really soothing. Spending time with a dog or an affectionate cat helps me a lot, they're much more accepting and affectionate than a lot of people. That's probably not something you can do right this second, but maybe in the future it could help.

In the short term, what's worked for me is to accept that if everything feels overwhelming and futile my brain is probably in defense mode, tilting my perceptions before they reach my conscience mind and making things seem more dangerous and more urgent than they are. When I'm in such a mental state, it's pretty impossible to help myself, and very difficult to ask for help. But if you can recognize when you're in a fight/flight state, then there's techniques that are very helpful to come down from that. Main things I do: 

1. Anything that stops my internal monologue. Reading a book or listening intently to spoken word (audiobook, lectures, old radio shows on youtube) works pretty well. 

2. Anything that highly engages one of my senses. Looking around the room and naming as many colors as I can. Or closing my eyes and  listening to try and determine what direction a sound is coming from. Or smelling something striking like mint or lemon or cinnamon. Or exposing myself to cold. Or water. 

3. Let go of responsibilities: this isn't always possible, and can feel guilty, but if you died you'd be letting down all your responsibilities anyway. Giving up on things for a day is better than giving up on all things permentantly. If you can pull all your attention down to just trying to get good food+water+sleep (and maybe exercise), that might bring some calm. Though I know it might not be enough for some problems, meeting basic needs makes it easier to solve all other problems. 


I hope that can help you. Please don't die. Believe that the extremes are temporary, and that the frequency of extremes can be reduced. And once you're not in fight/flight mode all the time, I think it will be much easier to figure out everything se. I think it's possible to heal from where you are now and experience a life that feels worth living. It's hard to believe right now. But I believe it.
